intro: Liszt’s Second Hungarian Rhapsody begins with a grave piano summons and ends in a rush of F♯-major octaves. Martha Goldstein plays the whole piece, including the long slow half that makes the dance feel so headlong.

sections.label: A · Lassan: the piano speaks
sections.mNote: C♯ major opens the door to C♯ minor

sections.label: A′ · Lassan: minor and major
sections.mNote: The slow phrases turn between dark and bright keys

sections.label: B · Friska: the dance begins
sections.mNote: Repeated figures begin quietly, then gather speed

sections.label: Link · A pause before the sprint
sections.mNote: The score returns to F♯ minor and allows a cadenza

sections.label: Coda · F♯-major octaves
sections.mNote: Prestissimo octaves race up and down the keyboard

cues.title: Major first, then minor
cues.text: The piano opens on a C♯-major chord, although C♯ minor is the slow section’s home. Within six bars the minor has taken hold. This is the Lassan, the rhapsody’s slow half, with the freedom of a speaker who can stop in the middle of a sentence.
cues.evidence: The opening major chord, establishment of C♯ minor by bar 6 and Lassan form are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune in Liszt’s notebook
cues.text: In 1846 Liszt writes down the opening tune after hearing someone play it. Five years later it appears at the head of this rhapsody, published by Bartholf Senff and dedicated to Count László Teleki.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard identifies the tune in Liszt’s 1846 sketchbook: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. Publisher, 1851 publication and dedication: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2.

cues.title: Minor and major
cues.text: The Lassan keeps turning from C♯ minor towards C♯ major and E major. Its grave phrases have bright, capricious neighbours. Liszt saves the steady dancing pulse for the second half.
cues.evidence: The account of the Lassan’s keys and contrasting passages is at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Songs played by Romani bands
cues.text: Liszt’s rhapsodies bring the songs and dances played by Romani bands to the concert piano. The musicians improvise on melodies that include published popular songs. Liszt even intends his book about Romani music in Hungary as a preface to the rhapsodies.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard discusses composed melodies, Romani improvisation and Liszt’s intended preface in his Hyperion notes: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.

cues.title: The dance starts quietly
cues.text: The Friska begins in F♯ minor, quietly, on a C♯-major chord. A tune remembered from the Lassan acquires a dancing step. Tonic and dominant chords alternate beneath it as the music gathers speed towards the main tune in F♯ major.
cues.evidence: The Friska’s opening harmony, recalled theme and move to F♯ major are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pupil gets another ending
cues.text: In his last years Liszt writes a cadenza and a new coda for his pupil Toni Raab. For Lina Schmalhausen he supplies further additions. Even this much-played rhapsody remains something he can reshape at the piano with a pupil beside him.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard documents Liszt’s additions for Toni Raab and Lina Schmalhausen: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. These are facts about the work’s history; Goldstein’s cadenza text is unidentified.

cues.title: Room for the pianist
cues.text: Near the end, F♯ minor returns and the dance pauses over a recollection of the Lassan. Liszt writes Cadenza ad libitum: the pianist may add a cadenza here. Rachmaninoff and d’Albert both take up the invitation and write their own.
cues.evidence: The F♯-minor recollection and cadenza marking are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. Cadenzas by Rachmaninoff and d’Albert: Leslie Howard, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Octaves across the keyboard
cues.text: The final Prestissimo is in F♯ major. Octaves climb and plunge across almost the whole keyboard, with a crescendo driving them towards the closing chords. The slow opening’s C♯ has become the dominant of this new home.
cues.evidence: The final F♯-major Prestissimo, crescendo and ascending and descending octaves are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: C♯ becomes the dance’s dominant
transitions.how: The Lassan’s C♯-minor world opens into F♯ minor. The Friska starts quietly on C♯ major, now the dominant chord, and recalls a tune from the slow section. Repeated piano figures establish the dance while tonic and dominant alternate underneath.
transitions.evidence: The Lassan–Friska join and its harmony are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.

transitions.title: The Lassan interrupts the dance
transitions.to: Link · A pause before the sprint
transitions.how: Before the final Prestissimo, the piano turns back to F♯ minor and recalls another tune from the Lassan. The dance relaxes into this slower recollection; Liszt then leaves space for a cadenza with the marking Cadenza ad libitum.
transitions.evidence: The late F♯-minor recollection and optional cadenza are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The boundary marks the broader late passage; the cadenza played here is unidentified.

transitions.title: Prestissimo in F♯ major
transitions.from: Link · A pause before the sprint
transitions.how: After the space for a cadenza, Liszt restores F♯ major and marks the piano Prestissimo. Rising and falling octaves fill the keyboard. The crescendo continues into the final chords in F♯ major.
transitions.evidence: The score’s final Prestissimo, octave runs and F♯-major close are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
